title: BRONZE BUTLER
summary: BRONZE BUTLER is an espionage cluster that public reporting associates with state interests and that vendors also track as Tick and REDBALDKNIGHT. Reporting describes activity dating back more than a decade against organisations in Japan and other parts of Asia, with a heavy emphasis on obtaining intellectual property and project documentation from technology and industrial firms. Its access method has been conventional but effective: spear phishing with malicious documents, sometimes paired with a software vulnerability, delivered alongside credible business lures. Public analyses have highlighted custom backdoors that store instructions inside image files and the use of legitimate file sharing services as relay points, which lets the group blend with ordinary web traffic. Persistence has been maintained through scheduled tasks and services rather than exotic techniques. The common misunderstanding is that encryption hides everything; metadata such as connection timing, referrer patterns, and the parent process of a document reader remains visible, and it is often the only evidence available when the payload is only ever in memory.

beginner.definition: BRONZE BUTLER is a name for a group that steals business secrets. Public reports describe them taking technical documents from companies in Japan and across Asia. Some vendors call the group Tick. Their work is quiet spying rather than causing damage, and they often stay for a long time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen design documents and research can cost a company years of investment. This group mostly uses common methods such as email with harmful attachments, so ordinary staff can be the entry point. They hide their messages inside image files and normal websites, which means simple checks may not notice. Understanding their habits helps you look for the small clues that remain.
howItWorks: The attacker writes a business email that fits the target company's work.
A document is attached and opened by an employee who sees nothing unusual.
The document starts a small program and then stays in the computer memory.
Hidden orders are stored inside image files and picked up from normal sites.
The intruder looks for design files, plans, and research documents.
Scheduled tasks keep the access alive across restarts and cleanups.
beginner.example: Imagine a courier who never carries a suspicious parcel. He walks past the desk carrying a framed picture. Nobody inspects a picture. Inside the frame is a written message for someone in the building. He collects replies the same way, one picture at a time. The frame is a normal image file and the message is the attacker's instruction.
takeaways: Files that are never written to disk can still leave useful evidence.
Watch for document programs starting unexpected network connections.
Protect design and research documents as closely as customer data.

objectives: Explain how command and control data can be embedded inside image files.
Describe the limitations of fileless or in-memory execution for investigators.
Explain why legitimate file sharing services complicate network detection.
Identify process ancestry evidence created by a malicious document.
Assess the business impact of intellectual property theft in Asia-focused espionage.
